claim: Purified S. oneidensis OMVs have a uniform single membrane phenotype with an approximate diameter of 225 nm.
source: Cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) tomographic reconstruction slices of the purified samples used to assess membrane morphology showed uniform OMVs with the characteristic single membrane phenotype and an approximate diameter of 225 nm (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated measurement from cryo-TEM imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: S. oneidensis OMVs exhibit redox activity with a prominent redox peak at a midpoint potential of 66 mV vs. SHE.
source: First derivative analysis (Figure 1B, inset) revealed a prominent redox peak with a midpoint potential of 66 mV and a smaller peak at –25 mV vs. a standard hydrogen reference electrode (SHE), consistent with the characteristics of multiheme cytochromes such as MtrC/OmcA (Xu et al., 2018; Okamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 1B with citation to previous work on multiheme cytochromes.

claim: BdpA is significantly enriched in S. oneidensis OMVs compared to the outer membrane.
source: Several proteins significantly enriched in the vesicles were identified that could contribute to OMV formation, including a putative murein transglycosylase (SO_2040), the peptidoglycan degradation enzyme holin (SO_2971), cell division coordinator CpoB (SO_2746), and a highly enriched putative BAR domain-containing protein encoded by the gene at open reading frame SO_1507, hereafter named BAR domain-like protein A (BdpA) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Proteomics comparison shown in Figure 1C volcano plot identifying enriched proteins.

claim: BdpA contains a predicted BAR domain spanning amino acids 276 to 451.
source: The C-terminal BAR domain of BdpA is predicted to span an alpha helical region from AA 276 to 451 (E-value = 2.96e-03); however, since the identification of the protein is based on homology to the eukaryotic BAR domain consensus sequence (cd07307), it is possible that the BAR domain region extends beyond these bounds (Figure 1D).
evidence: Bioinformatics prediction based on homology to eukaryotic BAR domain consensus sequence.

claim: BdpA is predicted to exist as antiparallel alpha-helical dimers.
source: Coiled-coil prediction (Vincent et al., 2013) suggests that BdpA exists in an oligomeric state of antiparallel alpha-helical dimers, as is the case for all known BAR domain proteins (Frost et al., 2007; Linkner et al., 2014; Cui et al., 2013; Henne et al., 2007).
evidence: Coiled-coil prediction with citation to known BAR domain protein structures.

claim: BdpA has an N-terminal signal peptide with predicted cleavage sites between amino acids 22 and 23.
source: BdpA has an N-terminal signal peptide with predicted cleavage sites between amino acids 22 and 23, suggesting non-cytoplasmic localization (Figure 1D).
evidence: Signal peptide prediction analysis suggesting subcellular localization.

claim: BdpA contains a galactose-binding domain-like region positioned immediately downstream of the signal peptide.
source: A galactose-binding domain-like region positioned immediately downstream of the signal peptide supports lipid targeting activity seen in other BAR domain proteins, such as the eukaryotic sorting nexins (van Weering and Cullen, 2014).
evidence: Domain prediction with comparison to eukaryotic BAR domain proteins.

claim: The predicted BdpA dimer has an intrinsically curved structure with positively charged residues along the concave surface.
source: Protein dimerization models were similarly generated using docking2 (Lyskov and Gray, 2008; Chaudhury et al., 2011; Lyskov et al., 2013), revealing an intrinsically curved dimer with positively charged residues along the concave surface (Figure 1F).
evidence: Ab initio structure prediction shown in Figure 1F.

claim: WT S. oneidensis OMVs have an average diameter of 190 nm with a standard deviation of ± 21 nm.
source: WT OMVs had an average diameter of 190 nm with little variability in the population (standard deviation [s.d.] = ± 21 nm), while the diameters of ΔbdpA OMVs were distributed over a wider range with a significantly different average value of 280 nm (p = 0.0375, Student's t-test, s.d. = ± 131 nm) (Figure 2A right).
evidence: DLS measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ΔbdpA OMVs have an average diameter of 280 nm with a standard deviation of ± 131 nm.
source: WT OMVs had an average diameter of 190 nm with little variability in the population (standard deviation [s.d.] = ± 21 nm), while the diameters of ΔbdpA OMVs were distributed over a wider range with a significantly different average value of 280 nm (p = 0.0375, Student's t-test, s.d. = ± 131 nm) (Figure 2A right).
evidence: DLS measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ΔbdpA+ bdpA complement strain produces OMVs with an average diameter of 136 nm with a standard deviation of ± 4 nm.
source: The average diameter of OMVs from the ΔbdpA+ bdpA strain was 136 nm (s.d. = ± 4 nm), which was significantly different than WT (p = <0.001).
evidence: DLS measurements with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The absence of bdpA results in loss of control over vesicle size distribution.
source: The large difference in standard deviations between WT and ΔbdpA indicates a loss of control over the size of vesicles in the absence of bdpA.
evidence: Statistical analysis of DLS data comparing variances between strains.

claim: BdpA strongly influences vesicle diameter.
source: These results suggest that BdpA strongly influences vesicle diameter.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from DLS measurements showing significant differences in vesicle size distributions.

claim: There is no significant difference in the overall frequency of OME production between WT and ΔbdpA strains during perfusion flow.
source: The average proportion of cells displaying either an OMV or OME relative to all cells was calculated for both strains. No significant difference was observed between the WT and ΔbdpA strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantification from perfusion flow microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ΔbdpA strain produces a significantly higher proportion of large vesicles (>300 nm diameter) compared to WT.
source: The ΔbdpA strain had a significantly higher proportion of cells producing large vesicles than the WT (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantification from perfusion flow microscopy shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance (p < 0.0001).

claim: At 90 min post-attachment, WT OMEs appear as mostly narrow chains or tubule-like structures.
source: At 90 min, OMEs from WT cells appeared as mostly narrow chains or tubule-like structures, and were seldom interspersed with lobed regions (Figure 3E, top), consistent with previous cryo-TEM analysis of S. oneidensis OMEs under similar conditions (Subramanian et al., 2018).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 3E with citation to previous work.

claim: At 90 min post-attachment, ΔbdpA OMEs have prevalent lobed regions with irregular curvature.
source: OMEs from ΔbdpA cells had prevalent lobed regions with irregular curvature, but a few tubules were also observed (Figure 3E, middle).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At 90 min post-attachment, ΔbdpA+ bdpA OMEs are narrow tubules evenly interspersed with slight constriction points.
source: OMEs from the ΔbdpA+ bdpA complement strain were narrow tubules evenly interspersed with slight constriction points or 'junction densities' (Subramanian et al., 2018) extending from cells, along with prevalent bulging or blebbing of the outer membrane (Figure 3E, bottom).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 3E with citation to previous work.

claim: At 3 hr post-attachment, WT OMEs consistently display tubule structures or narrow chains of symmetric curvature.
source: At 3 hr, the WT strain consistently displayed tubule OMEs (depicted in Figure 3F, top panel) or narrow chains of symmetric curvature.
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: At 3 hr post-attachment, ΔbdpA OMEs appear as lobed, disordered vesicle chains with irregular curvature.
source: The ΔbdpA OMEs appear as lobed, disordered vesicle chains with irregular curvature compared to the WT, and vesicles can be observed branching laterally from lobes on the extensions (Figure 3F, middle panel).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Tubules were not observed in any ΔbdpA OMEs at 3 hr post-attachment.
source: Tubules were not observed in any ΔbdpA OMEs at 3 hr.
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations across multiple samples.

claim: At 3 hr post-attachment, ΔbdpA+ bdpA OMEs appear as narrow tubules of uniform curvature or as ordered vesicle chains.
source: OMEs from ΔbdpA+ bdpA cells appear as narrow tubules of a uniform curvature or as ordered vesicle chains similar to the WT strain (Figure 3F, bottom panel).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Overexpression of BdpA in WT S. oneidensis during planktonic growth results in OME formation prior to surface attachment.
source: DAPG (12.5 µM) was added to planktonic cultures (n = 3 biological replicates) freshly inoculated from overnight cultures of the WT strain harboring p452-bdpA (WT+ bdpA) and incubated for 1 hr prior to deposition on cover glass for imaging. OMEs were observed at the outset of imaging indicating they had already formed during the incubation period (Figure 4A, left panels, Video 6).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A following BdpA induction.

claim: OMEs from WT + bdpA strain after 2 hr planktonic induction appear as tubules or tubule-like segments interspersed with narrow vesicle chains.
source: The ultrastructure of OMEs from the WT + bdpA strain was examined by cryo-TEM 2 hr post-induction (n = 2 cultures). OMEs (n = 9 total OMEs observed) appeared as either tubules (6 out of 9 OMEs) or tubule-like segments interspersed with narrow vesicle chains proximal to the main cell body (3 out of 9 OMEs) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations shown in Figure 4B with quantification.

claim: Heterologous expression of BdpA in M. atlanticus CP1 results in OME production.
source: Cultures (n = 3 biological replicates for each strain) of WT and transformed M. atlanticus and E. coli BL21(DE3) were prepared in an identical manner to those used for S. oneidensis planktonic expression experiments described above. OMEs were observed in both strains harboring the p452-bdpA vector following induction of bdpA expression by DAPG (12.5 µM) for 1 hr prior to deposition on cover glass, and representative images are shown in Figure 4A (middle and right panels).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Heterologous expression of BdpA in E. coli BL21(DE3) results in OME production.
source: Cultures (n = 3 biological replicates for each strain) of WT and transformed M. atlanticus and E. coli BL21(DE3) were prepared in an identical manner to those used for S. oneidensis planktonic expression experiments described above. OMEs were observed in both strains harboring the p452-bdpA vector following induction of bdpA expression by DAPG (12.5 µM) for 1 hr prior to deposition on cover glass, and representative images are shown in Figure 4A (middle and right panels).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA cells display OMEs that appear as a web-like network of reticular membrane structures.
source: E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA cells (Figure 4A, right panels) also displayed OMEs; however, in most cases OMEs appeared as a web-like network of reticular membrane structures.
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OMEs are significantly more prevalent in all cells with the bdpA plasmid than WT cells.
source: OMEs were significantly more prevalent in all cells with the bdpA plasmid than WT cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantification from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis.

claim: E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA has the most cells associated with outer membrane structures per total number of cells.
source: The E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA strain had the most cells associated with outer membrane structures per total number of cells per field.
evidence: Quantification from fluorescence microscopy comparing different strains.

claim: S. oneidensis WT + bdpA and M. atlanticus CP1+ bdpA display more tubule-like OMEs than E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA.
source: S. oneidensis WT + bdpA and M. atlanticus CP1+ bdpA displayed more tubule-like OMEs than E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA (p = 1.1 × 10–5 and p = 0.035, respectively) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantification from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4D with statistical analysis.

claim: The majority of OMEs associated with E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA cells have a web-like, reticular morphology.
source: The majority of OMEs associated with E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA cells had the web-like, reticular morphology noted in Figure 4A, right panels (quantified in Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantification from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 52 BdpA homologs were identified by PSI-BLAST in Shewanella, Alishewanella, Rheinheimera, and Cellvibrio species.
source: Fifty-two BdpA homologs were identified by PSI-BLAST in most but not all species of Shewanella, as well as Alishewanella, Rheinheimera, and Cellvibrio.
evidence: PSI-BLAST search results identifying homologous proteins.

claim: Only 5 of 52 bacterial BdpA homologs were predicted to contain a BAR domain by the current Pfam HMM despite greater than 90% homology to S. oneidensis BdpA.
source: The current BAR domain Pfam HMM prediction analysis identified BAR domain features in only 5 of the 52 bacterial homologs despite greater than 90% homology to S. oneidensis BdpA.
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis comparing homology and domain prediction results.

claim: BdpA and its homologs form a cohesive clade separate from other bacterial membrane-associated proteins and cluster more closely with eukaryotic BAR domain-containing proteins.
source: In this maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree generated from this alignment, the BdpA sequences form a cohesive clade separate from other bacterial proteins that associate with membranes or influence curvature in vitro and instead clusters more closely with eukaryotic BAR domain-containing proteins (Figure 5).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: BdpA likely contains a functional, yet unique BAR domain based on phylogenetic analysis.
source: The maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree built from this alignment shows that BdpA and its homologs have branch lengths shorter than those between eukaryotic BAR domain-containing proteins, suggesting that BdpA likely contains a functional, yet unique BAR domain.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis comparing branch lengths.

claim: Induction of BdpA expression in the ΔbdpA+ bdpA strain results in attenuated growth.
source: Induction of BdpA expression in the ΔbdpA+ bdpA strain displayed attenuated growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BdpA could have redundant activity with FtsA during cell division.
source: It is possible that BdpA could have redundant activity with FtsA, another alpha-helical protein known to stabilize FtsZ during contractile ring formation and cell division (Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2005).
evidence: Speculation based on observed growth phenotype and known function of FtsA with citation.

claim: Crowding of BdpA at the membrane could potentially inhibit the ability of FtsA to interact with FtsZ.
source: Crowding of BdpA at the membrane could potentially inhibit the ability of FtsA to interact with FtsZ.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism of growth attenuation.

claim: S. oneidensis OMVs and OMEs are redox-active and can reduce extracellular iron, uranium, and technetium.
source: The production of OMVs and OMEs in S. oneidensis is well documented, particularly upon surface attachment (Chong et al., 2019; Subramanian et al., 2018; Pirbadian et al., 2014; Gorby et al., 2008), and previous measurements showed that both are redox-active and can reduce extracellular iron, uranium, and technetium (Gorby et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: OMEs transition between membrane blebs or OMVs into chains of vesicles and tubules.
source: OMEs transition between membrane blebs or OMVs into chains of vesicles and tubules (Pirbadian et al., 2014); however, little is known about the mechanism controlling OME formation, shape, and curvature.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work.

claim: BAR domain proteins generate membrane curvature through electrostatic interactions between positively charged amino acids and negatively charged lipids.
source: In eukaryotes, Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domain-containing proteins generate membrane curvature through electrostatic interactions between positively charged amino acids and negatively charged lipids scaffolding the membrane along the intrinsically curved surface of the antiparallel coiled-coil protein dimers (Peter et al., 2004; Frost et al., 2007; Shimada et al., 2007; Weissenhorn, 2005).
evidence: Statement about eukaryotic BAR domain protein mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claim: The extent of accumulation of BAR domain proteins at a specific site can influence the degree of the resultant membrane curvature.
source: The extent of accumulation of BAR domain proteins at a specific site can influence the degree of the resultant membrane curvature (Simunovic et al., 2015), and tubulation events arise as a consequence of BAR domain multimerization in conjunction with lipid binding (Mim et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about BAR domain protein function supported by citations.

claim: Tubulation events arise as a consequence of BAR domain multimerization in conjunction with lipid binding.
source: The extent of accumulation of BAR domain proteins at a specific site can influence the degree of the resultant membrane curvature (Simunovic et al., 2015), and tubulation events arise as a consequence of BAR domain multimerization in conjunction with lipid binding (Mim et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about BAR domain protein function supported by citation.

claim: Characterization of a functional bacterial BAR domain protein has not been reported prior to this study.
source: Despite our knowledge of numerous eukaryotic BAR domain-containing proteins spanning a variety of modes of curvature formation, membrane localizations, and subtypes, characterization of a functional bacterial BAR domain protein has yet to be reported.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the work based on literature review.

claim: Previously described membrane curvature-promoting proteins in bacteria are unrelated to BAR domain proteins.
source: Previously described membrane curvature-promoting proteins in bacteria are unrelated to BAR domain proteins or contain features ancillary to eukaryotic BAR domain protein function, such as amphipathic alpha helices (SpoVM, PmtA) (Danne et al., 2017a; Danne et al., 2017b; Gill et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017), GTPase-associated signaling (FtsZ) (Löwe and Amos, 1998), or positive curvature localization (SpoVM, MamY) (Gill et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Toro-Nahuelpan et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous work on bacterial membrane proteins.

claim: Actin-like, dynamin-like, and ESCRT-II-like proteins have been previously discovered in bacteria and archaea.
source: However, actin-like (van den Ent and Löwe, 2000; Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2005), dynamin-like (Low and Löwe, 2006), and ESCRT-II-like (Junglas, 2021; Liu, 2020) proteins have been previously discovered in bacteria and archaea, suggesting that vesicle formation and tubule biogenesis can be achieved through evolutionarily conserved mechanisms.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous discoveries.

claim: S. oneidensis is a model organism for extracellular electron transfer (EET).
source: S. oneidensis is a model organism for extracellular electron transfer (EET), a mode of respiration whereby metabolic electrons reduce exogenous terminal electron acceptors such as metals and electrodes.
evidence: Statement about S. oneidensis as a model organism based on established knowledge.

claim: S. oneidensis OMEs are more commonly observed in surface-attached cells than planktonic cells.
source: S. oneidensis OMEs are more commonly observed in surface-attached cells than planktonic cells (Chong et al., 2019; Subramanian et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BdpA was identified as expressed in planktonic cultures by proteomics.
source: BdpA was identified as expressed in planktonic cultures by proteomics, and its absence resulted in larger size vesicles during planktonic growth suggesting it may play a role in constraining membrane shape.
evidence: Statement based on proteomics data from planktonic cultures.

claim: The absence of BdpA resulted in larger size vesicles during planktonic growth.
source: BdpA was identified as expressed in planktonic cultures by proteomics, and its absence resulted in larger size vesicles during planktonic growth suggesting it may play a role in constraining membrane shape.
evidence: Statement based on DLS measurements comparing WT and ΔbdpA strains.

claim: Similar membrane sculpting phenotypes showing a mixture of tubules and pearled segments were observed from in vitro cryo-TEM experiments using liposomes and purified F-BAR protein Pacsin1 from eukaryotic cells.
source: Similar membrane sculpting phenotypes showing a mixture of tubules and pearled, 'beads on a string' segments within the same field of view were observed previously from in vitro cryo-TEM experiments using liposomes and purified F-BAR protein Pacsin1 from eukaryotic cells (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison to previous work on eukaryotic F-BAR proteins with citation.

claim: BdpA may constrict or scaffold OMVs produced during planktonic growth into OMEs.
source: Thus, as predicted, BdpA may constrict or scaffold OMVs produced during planktonic growth into OMEs (Chong et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on observed phenotypes with citation to previous work.

claim: Marinobacter and Shewanella are of the same phylogenetic order (Alteromonadales).
source: Marinobacter and Shewanella are of the same phylogenetic order (Alteromonadales), and M. atlanticus has been used for expression of other S. oneidensis proteins (Bird et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about phylogenetic relationship with citation.

claim: E. coli strain BL21(DE3) is optimized for protein overexpression.
source: E. coli strain BL21(DE3) is optimized for protein overexpression.
evidence: Statement about E. coli strain characteristics based on established knowledge.

claim: M. atlanticus CP1+ bdpA OMEs ranged from small membrane blebs to tubules extending beyond 10 µm in length from the surface of the cell.
source: M. atlanticus CP1+ bdpA OMEs ranged from small membrane blebs to tubules extending beyond 10 µm in length from the surface of the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of S. oneidensis BdpA results in membrane remodeling into structures resembling those associated with the presence of BAR domain-containing proteins from in vitro eukaryotic BAR protein experiments.
source: These results show that expression of S. oneidensis BdpA results in membrane remodeling into structures resembling those associated with the presence of BAR domain-containing proteins from in vitro eukaryotic BAR protein experiments (Ayton et al., 2009; Simunovic et al., 2013; Noguchi, 2016).
evidence: Conclusion based on observed phenotypes with citations to previous work on eukaryotic BAR proteins.

claim: BdpA barely met the criteria to be assigned as matching the BAR domain via PSSM models.
source: Overall, BdpA barely met the criteria to be assigned as matching the BAR domain via PSSM models.
evidence: Statement based on bioinformatics analysis results.

claim: The sequence conservation between BdpA and the existing BAR domain consensus sequence is at the cusp of a positive hit by the HMM.
source: This indicates that while sequence homology between BdpA and the existing BAR domain consensus sequence predicted the BAR domain region in BdpA using hmmer or NCBI tools, the sequence conservation is at the cusp of a positive hit by the HMM since other closely related (>90% homology) BdpA orthologs were not predicted to contain a BAR domain by this method.
evidence: Statement based on bioinformatics analysis comparing homology and domain prediction results.

claim: The eukaryotic protein most similar to BdpA has 27% amino acid identity and is a putative centrosomal protein in the ant Vollenhovia emeryi.
source: The eukaryotic protein that is most similar to BdpA (27% amino acid identity) is a putative centrosomal protein in the ant Vollenhovia emeryi (accession #: XP_011868153) that is predicted to contain an amino terminal C2 membrane-binding domain and a carboxy-terminal SMC domain within a coiled-coil region.
evidence: Statement based on PSI-BLAST search results.

claim: The homology between BdpA and the ant centrosomal protein could be due to convergent evolution.
source: Alternatively, the homology could be due to convergent evolution because of the necessary spacing of polar amino acids to maintain the coiled-coil structure in both BdpA and XP_011868153.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary relationship based on structural considerations.

claim: The evolutionary origin of the BdpA clade of protein remains unclear from the sequences currently available.
source: The evolutionary origin of this clade of protein remains unclear from the sequences currently available.
evidence: Statement based on phylogenetic analysis limitations.

claim: It is possible that BdpA arose as a result of convergent evolution due to selection of positively charged amino acids at key locations along the helices.
source: It is possible that BdpA arose as a result of convergent evolution due to selection of positively charged amino acids at key locations along the helices.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary origin based on structural features.

claim: There is a possibility that the predicted BAR domain-containing region arose as a result of horizontal gene transfer from a eukaryote.
source: There is also a possibility that the predicted BAR domain-containing region arose as a result of horizontal gene transfer from a eukaryote due to the prevalence of eukaryotic coiled-coil proteins with predicted homology to BdpA after two iterations of PSI-BLAST.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary origin based on PSI-BLAST results.

claim: Conservation of BAR domain proteins supports the notion that three-dimensional organization of proteins in lipid structures is as important to bacteria as it is eukaryotes.
source: Conservation of BAR domain proteins supports the notion that three-dimensional organization of proteins in lipid structures is as important to bacteria as it is eukaryotes, and suggests that additional novel bacterial BAR domain-like proteins are waiting to be discovered.
evidence: Inference based on the discovery of BdpA and its homologs.

claim: S. oneidensis expresses a functional membrane sculpting protein with BAR domain-like activity and homology, which is the first identified and characterized in bacteria.
source: S. oneidensis expresses a functional membrane sculpting protein with BAR domain-like activity and homology, which is the first identified and characterized in bacteria.
evidence: Summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: Enrichment of BdpA in the redox-active OMVs and BdpA-mediated sculpting of the OMVs into a uniform diameter suggests overlapping mechanistic functionality with eukaryotic BAR proteins in the context of vesicle constriction.
source: Enrichment of BdpA in the redox-active OMVs and BdpA-mediated sculpting of the OMVs into a uniform diameter suggests overlapping mechanistic functionality with eukaryotic BAR proteins in the context of vesicle constriction (Daumke et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on proteomics and DLS data with citation to eukaryotic BAR protein function.

claim: Membrane constriction activity of BdpA was confirmed through cryo-EM images that depicted disordered tubules in the absence of BdpA.
source: Membrane constriction activity of BdpA was confirmed through cryo-EM images that depicted disordered tubules in the absence of BdpA.
evidence: Statement based on cryo-TEM observations of ΔbdpA strain.

claim: Variation in OMEs with BdpA ranged from ordered, narrow vesicle chains of a consistent diameter to stable tubules.
source: Variation in OMEs with BdpA ranged from ordered, narrow vesicle chains of a consistent diameter to stable tubules.
evidence: Statement based on cryo-TEM observations of WT and complement strains.

claim: The closest phylogenetic eukaryotic BAR domain subtype to BdpA is F-BAR domains.
source: The closest phylogenetic eukaryotic BAR domain subtype to BdpA, F-BAR domains, exhibits similar variation in tubule morphology, depending upon the orientation of the tip-to-tip oligomerization around the tubules (Frost et al., 2007; Shimada et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement based on phylogenetic analysis with citations to F-BAR protein studies.

claim: The presence of the predicted galactose-binding domain-like region at the N-terminal end of BdpA suggests possible localization to the outer membrane.
source: While the presence of the predicted galactose-binding domain-like region at the N-terminal end of the protein suggests possible localization to the outer membrane, we cannot rule out that membrane sculpting phenotypes observed with BdpA are an indirect consequence of binding to LPS or through association with periplasmic components, such as peptidoglycan, at this time.
evidence: Inference based on domain prediction with acknowledgment of alternative possibilities.

claim: The discovery of BdpA and its homologs presents a critical step in understanding the impact of membrane sculpting proteins with BAR domain-like activity on extracellular membrane structures.
source: Ultimately, the discovery of BdpA and its homologs presents a critical step in understanding the impact of membrane sculpting proteins with BAR domain-like activity on extracellular membrane structures.
evidence: Summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Bacterial outer membrane vesicle (OMV) formation is ubiquitous and has many documented functions.
source: Bacterial outer membrane vesicle (OMV) formation is ubiquitous and has many documented functions (Toyofuku et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to review article.

claim: Outer membrane extensions (OMEs) are less commonly observed than OMVs.
source: Outer membrane extensions (OMEs) are less commonly observed.
evidence: Statement based on literature review.

claim: OMEs remain attached to the cell.
source: OMEs remain attached to the cell, and various morphologies can be seen extending from single cells including Myxococcus xanthus (Remis et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2014), flavobacterium strain Hel3_A1_48 (Fischer et al., 2019), Vibrio vulnificus (Hampton et al., 2017), Francisella novicida (Sampath et al., 2018), as cell-cell connections in Bacillus subtilis (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Dubey et al., 2016; Dubey and Ben-Yehuda, 2011), and Escherichia coli (Pande et al., 2015), and as redox-active nanowires in Shewanella oneidensis (Chong et al., 2019; Subramanian et al., 2018; Pirbadian et al., 2014; Gorby et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Researchers suspect that pathways for OMV and OME formation have some mechanistic overlap.
source: Researchers suspect that pathways for OMV and OME formation have some mechanistic overlap (Fischer et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: It is proposed that proteins are necessary to stabilize bacterial cell membrane curvature during the formation of OMVs and OMEs.
source: Bacterial cell membrane curvature is observed during the formation of OMVs and OMEs, and it is proposed that proteins are necessary to stabilize these structures (Bohuszewicz et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Several bacterial proteins have demonstrated membrane tubule formation capabilities in vitro.
source: Several bacterial proteins have demonstrated membrane tubule formation capabilities in vitro (Tanaka et al., 2010; Danne et al., 2017a; Danne et al., 2017b; Danne et al., 2015; Low et al., 2009; Low and Löwe, 2006), but despite the growing number of reports, proteins involved in shaping bacterial membranes into OMV/OMEs in living cells have yet to be identified.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Proteins involved in shaping bacterial membranes into OMV/OMEs in living cells have not been identified prior to this study.
source: Several bacterial proteins have demonstrated membrane tubule formation capabilities in vitro (Tanaka et al., 2010; Danne et al., 2017a; Danne et al., 2017b; Danne et al., 2015; Low et al., 2009; Low and Löwe, 2006), but despite the growing number of reports, proteins involved in shaping bacterial membranes into OMV/OMEs in living cells have yet to be identified.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the work based on literature review.

claim: MtrCAB cytochromes were present in the OMVs as well as the outer membrane.
source: MtrCAB cytochromes were present in the OMVs as well as the outer membrane, supporting redox activity of OMVs observed by CV.
evidence: Proteomics data supporting the redox activity measurements.

claim: 328 proteins were significantly enriched in the vesicles compared to the outer membrane.
source: The proteome of the purified OMVs showed 328 proteins were significantly enriched in the vesicles as compared to the outer membrane, and 314 proteins were significantly excluded from the vesicles (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Proteomics data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 314 proteins were significantly excluded from the vesicles compared to the outer membrane.
source: The proteome of the purified OMVs showed 328 proteins were significantly enriched in the vesicles as compared to the outer membrane, and 314 proteins were significantly excluded from the vesicles (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Proteomics data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The S. oneidensis rough-type lipopolysaccharide (LPS) contains 2-acetamido-2-deoxy-D-galactose.
source: The S. oneidensis rough-type lipopolysaccharide (LPS) contains 2-acetamido-2-deoxy-D-galactose (Vinogradov et al., 2003), which could suggest localization of the protein to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane.
evidence: Statement about LPS composition supported by citation.

claim: The maximum optical density was lower for the ΔbdpA+ bdpA strain compared to the wild-type (WT) and ΔbdpA strains when grown with 1.25 or 12.5 µM DAPG.
source: Growth curves for each strain show that the maximum optical density was lower for the ΔbdpA+ bdpA strain compared to the wild-type (WT) and ΔbdpA strains when grown with 1.25 or 12.5 µM DAPG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference in ferrihydrite reduction was observed between WT and ΔbdpA strains.
source: Ferrihydrite reduction assays were also performed to determine if EET was compromised in the bdpA deletion strain or induced complement. No difference was observed between WT or ΔbdpA, but ΔbdpA+ bdpA cells reduced ferrihydrite at a slightly delayed rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Ferrihydrite reduction assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ΔbdpA+ bdpA cells reduced ferrihydrite at a slightly delayed rate compared to WT.
source: Ferrihydrite reduction assays were also performed to determine if EET was compromised in the bdpA deletion strain or induced complement. No difference was observed between WT or ΔbdpA, but ΔbdpA+ bdpA cells reduced ferrihydrite at a slightly delayed rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Ferrihydrite reduction assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: If BdpA is involved in membrane remodeling, cell division could be compromised in the complement strain when expression of bdpA is not under native control.
source: These results suggest that if BdpA is involved in membrane remodeling, cell division could be compromised in the complement strain when expression of bdpA is not under native control, resulting in delayed growth.
evidence: Inference based on observed growth phenotypes.

claim: Growth and iron reduction were affected in the ΔbdpA+ bdpA cultures even if no inducer was added, indicating leaky expression from the phlF promoter.
source: Growth and iron reduction were affected in the ΔbdpA+ bdpA cultures even if no inducer was added, indicating leaky expression from the phlF promoter.
evidence: Observation from growth curves and iron reduction assays.

claim: There is no statistically significant difference in the overall frequency of OMEs between WT, ΔbdpA, and ΔbdpA+ bdpA strains in static cultures at 3 hr post-deposition.
source: Similar to perfusion flow experiments, no statistically significant difference in the overall frequency of OMEs was observed between strains (Figure 3b).
evidence: Quantification from fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: Tubules and narrow chains observed in the WT + bdpA mixed phenotype resembled those at 3 hr in surface-attached cells of the WT strain.
source: Tubules and narrow chains observed in this mixed phenotype resembled those at 3 hr in surface-attached cells of the WT strain, confirming that the OME structures observed during planktonic induction are single-membrane periplasmic extensions and not cytoplasmic bacterial nanotubes (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Dubey et al., 2016; Dubey and Ben-Yehuda, 2011; Pande et al., 2015; Pospíšil et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison of cryo-TEM observations with citations to previous work on bacterial nanotubes.

claim: The OME structures observed during planktonic induction are single-membrane periplasmic extensions and not cytoplasmic bacterial nanotubes.
source: Tubules and narrow chains observed in this mixed phenotype resembled those at 3 hr in surface-attached cells of the WT strain, confirming that the OME structures observed during planktonic induction are single-membrane periplasmic extensions and not cytoplasmic bacterial nanotubes (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Dubey et al., 2016; Dubey and Ben-Yehuda, 2011; Pande et al., 2015; Pospíšil et al., 2020).
evidence: Cryo-TEM observations with citations to previous work distinguishing OMEs from nanotubes.

claim: Additional biochemical and biophysical assays are needed to further elucidate the effect of BdpA on membrane sculpting.
source: Additional biochemical and biophysical assays beyond the scope of this initial manuscript are needed to further elucidate the effect of BdpA on membrane sculpting.
evidence: Statement about future work needed.

claim: M. atlanticus has been used for expression of other S. oneidensis proteins.
source: Marinobacter and Shewanella are of the same phylogenetic order (Alteromonadales), and M. atlanticus has been used for expression of other S. oneidensis proteins (Bird et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: OMEs were not observed in WT cells for M. atlanticus and E. coli strains.
source: WT cells for each strain had uniform, continuous cell membranes.
evidence: Observation from fluorescence microscopy of control strains.

claim: The E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA strain had the most cells associated with outer membrane structures per total number of cells per field, which was expected since this E. coli strain was designed for protein overexpression.
source: The E. coli BL21(DE3)+ bdpA strain had the most cells associated with outer membrane structures per total number of cells per field. This result was expected, since this E. coli strain was designed for protein overexpression.
evidence: Quantification from fluorescence microscopy with explanation based on strain characteristics.

claim: In the initial PSI-BLAST round, 24 proteins were found from other organisms identified as Shewanella with high conservation.
source: In the initial round, 24 proteins were found from other organisms identified as Shewanella with a high conservation among the proteins and another 28 proteins were found in more distant bacterial species that had an amino acid identity of 65–44%.
evidence: PSI-BLAST search results.

claim: A second PSI-BLAST iteration identified an additional 28 proteins in more distant bacterial species with 65–44% amino acid identity to BdpA.
source: In the initial round, 24 proteins were found from other organisms identified as Shewanella with a high conservation among the proteins and another 28 proteins were found in more distant bacterial species that had an amino acid identity of 65–44%.
evidence: PSI-BLAST search results.

claim: A second PSI-BLAST iteration identified proteins from the eukaryotic phylum Arthropoda that were annotated as being centrosomal proteins.
source: A second iteration identified a few proteins from more distantly related bacterial species, followed by proteins from the eukaryotic phylum Arthropoda that were annotated as being centrosomal proteins.
evidence: PSI-BLAST search results.

claim: Only five of the proteins from the PSI-BLAST search returned hits to the PSSM of the BAR cd07307.
source: Only five of the proteins from the search returned hits to the position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM) of the BAR cd07307, but two did not have any unique residues within the BAR domain.
evidence: PSI-BLAST and PSSM analysis results.

claim: The rest of the BdpA homologs had enough differences to fail to match the BAR model despite all having greater than 44% amino acid identity to the S. oneidensis BdpA sequence.
source: The rest of the protein homologs identified had enough differences to fail to match the BAR model despite all having greater than 44% amino acid identity to the S. oneidensis BdpA sequence.
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis comparing homology and domain prediction results.

claim: An attempt to build a hidden Markov model (HMM) using hmmer returned only the proteins that formed the model as good matches.
source: An attempt was made to build a hidden Markov model (HMM) using hmmer (Finn et al., 2011) to use for searching for other proteins that might match, but as with the PSI-BLAST search, only the proteins that formed the model were returned as good matches.
evidence: HMM analysis results with citation.

claim: The branch lengths and low bootstrap values supporting the placement of many of the BAR domain subtypes prevent direct inference of the evolutionary history of BAR domains.
source: However, the branch lengths and low bootstrap values supporting the placement of many of the BAR domain subtypes prevent us from directly inferring the evolutionary history of BAR domains.
evidence: Statement about limitations of phylogenetic analysis.

claim: If future comparative proteomics analysis of OME/OMVs demonstrates overlapping activity of BdpA with preferential cargo loading into OME/OMVs, it could hint at the evolutionary origins of vesicle-based protein trafficking.
source: Discovery of other putative bacterial BAR proteins would help to build this analysis, and if future comparative proteomics analysis of OME/OMVs demonstrates overlapping activity of BdpA with preferential cargo loading into OME/OMVs, it could hint at the evolutionary origins of vesicle-based protein trafficking.
evidence: Speculation about future work and implications.

claim: Additional novel bacterial BAR domain-like proteins are waiting to be discovered.
source: Conservation of BAR domain proteins supports the notion that three-dimensional organization of proteins in lipid structures is as important to bacteria as it is eukaryotes, and suggests that additional novel bacterial BAR domain-like proteins are waiting to be discovered.
evidence: Inference based on the discovery of BdpA and its homologs.

claim: Subsequent studies will include vesicle constriction into tubules in vitro with purified protein to ascertain the extent of functional mechanistic similarity of BdpA to other F-BAR proteins.
source: Subsequent studies will include vesicle constriction into tubules in vitro with purified protein to ascertain the extent of functional mechanistic similarity of BdpA to other F-BAR proteins.
evidence: Statement about planned future experiments.

claim: We cannot rule out that membrane sculpting phenotypes observed with BdpA are an indirect consequence of binding to LPS or through association with periplasmic components, such as peptidoglycan.
source: While the presence of the predicted galactose-binding domain-like region at the N-terminal end of the protein suggests possible localization to the outer membrane, we cannot rule out that membrane sculpting phenotypes observed with BdpA are an indirect consequence of binding to LPS or through association with periplasmic components, such as peptidoglycan, at this time.
evidence: Acknowledgment of alternative mechanisms.
